content: The Cochrane Oral Health group is conducting a series of systematic reviews on the accuracy of diagnostic tests for detecting and diagnosing dental caries. These reviews are part of a National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Cochrane Programme Grant Scheme and involve collaboration with the Complex Reviews Support Unit. The reviews will adhere to standard Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) methodologies and will be tailored to the specific diagnostic tests being evaluated. Dental caries is a disease process that can be stabilized and, in some cases, reversed if diagnosed and treated early in its progression. In some Scandinavian countries, programs have nearly eradicated caries, but these efforts require continuous daily work and have not been replicated in other populations. Despite these efforts, the 2015 Global Burden of Disease study identified dental caries as the most prevalent preventable condition worldwide, affecting 60% to 90% of children and the majority of adults globally. The global incidence of untreated caries was reported to be 2.4 billion in 2010, and despite reductions in some industrialized countries, the global incidence increased by 14% over five years to 2015, affecting over half a billion people. In the UK, the primary reason for hospital admissions among children aged 5 to 9 years is tooth extraction. Longitudinal studies have shown that early childhood caries increases the risk of severe caries later in life, with a trajectory of increasing disease severity. Untreated caries can lead to severe pain and infection, often requiring antibiotics. Dental anxiety, resulting from untreated caries and the need for invasive treatments, can discourage future dental visits, perpetuating a cycle of oral disease. If caries progresses, treatment options are limited to restoration or extraction, requiring repeated dental visits or even hospital care. The cost of treating caries is substantial; in the UK alone, the National Health Service (NHS) spends approximately £500 million annually on caries treatment. Additionally, hidden costs, such as productivity losses, are significant, estimated at $27 billion globally in 2010. Caries detection and diagnosis are typically performed during routine dental examinations by general dental practitioners in asymptomatic patients. However, caries detection can also be employed in secondary care settings, school or community screening projects, and epidemiological or research studies. The traditional method of detecting dental caries in clinical practice involves a visual-tactile examination, often supported by radiographic investigations. This combination is effective in detecting caries that have progressed into dentine and reached a threshold requiring restoration. Detecting caries earlier in the disease continuum could stabilize the disease or even allow for remineralization of the tooth surface, preventing the patient from entering a lifelong cycle of restoration. However, early caries is challenging to detect visually, and radiographs have limited ability to detect small changes in dental enamel. Detection and diagnosis at the initial (non-cavitated) and moderate (enamel cavitation) levels of caries are fundamental to promoting oral health and preventing oral disease. A wide variety of treatment options are available under NHS care at these different thresholds of disease, ranging from minimally invasive treatments, such as sealing the affected surface of the tooth or infiltrating the softer demineralized tissue with resins, to stepwise caries removal and restoration for extensive lesions. Advances in technology over the last two decades have introduced alternative methods of detection, such as advancements in radiography and the development of fluorescence, transillumination, and electrical conductance devices. These could potentially aid or replace the detection and diagnosis of caries at an early stage of decay, affording the patient less invasive treatment with less destruction of tooth tissue and potentially reducing the cost of care to both the patient and healthcare services. Dental caries is a disease process that can be arrested and sometimes reversed if diagnosed early enough. The term dental caries describes the mechanisms and symptoms of the breakdown of the tooth surface resulting from an imbalance in the activity within the biofilm (or dental plaque) in the oral cavity. This imbalance is especially related to pH levels, which are readily affected by the consumption of sugar, increasing acidity. Disease progression can be moderated by the influx of fluoride through toothpaste and other available fluoride sources. However, the levels of sugar consumption observed in many populations often outweigh the benefits of fluoride. Ultimately, carious lesions may develop and destroy the structure of the tooth. The most common surfaces for caries to manifest are on the biting (occlusal) surface or the tooth surface facing an adjacent tooth (approximal surfaces), although smooth surfaces on the flat exterior of teeth can also be affected. The severity of disease is defined by the depth of erosion of the tooth's structure and whether the lesion is active or arrested. Caries presenting at levels into tooth enamel have the potential to be stabilized or even reversed, whereas the progression of carious lesions into the dentine and pulp of the tooth will require restoration. Assessment of disease severity traditionally used in epidemiological and research studies has employed some variant of the DMFT (decayed, missing, and filled teeth) scale. Within the D (decayed) component, there are four clinically detectable thresholds applied as indicators for diagnosis and treatment planning, often labeled as D1, D2, D3, and D4. Typically, the D3 threshold has been used to determine the presence of caries. These four categories have formed the basis for expanded indices such as the International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS). Other available systems include the Nyvad system, Ekstrand-Ricketts-Kidd (ERK) system, British Association for the Study of Community Dentistry (BASCD), and the Dundee Selectable Threshold Method for caries diagnosis (DSTM). The ICDAS and DSTM systems both provide the opportunity to investigate initial caries (into enamel), which may confer benefits for preventative or non-operative treatment. There are many varied treatment options available to the dental clinician, dependent on the thresholds of observed disease. Initial caries can be treated without surgical intervention using preventative and remineralizing approaches such as plaque control, dietary advice, and application of fluoride. Minimally invasive treatments for initial caries are available, such as sealing the affected surface of the tooth or infiltrating the softer demineralized tissue with resins. High-risk patients with severe caries may require stepwise caries removal and restoration of extensive lesions. A caries management pathway, informed by diagnostic information, can be beneficial in guiding the clinician towards prevention or a treatment plan. One recently developed care pathway is the International Caries Classification and Management System (ICCMS), which presents three forms of management in the care pathway: preventative strategies for sound dentition, non-invasive treatment to arrest decay and encourage remineralization, and management of more severe caries through excavation and restoration or potentially extraction. At the core of this care pathway is the ability to detect early caries accurately and optimize preventative strategies. The detection and diagnosis of early caries remain challenging, and the likelihood of undiagnosed early disease is high. In such instances, the opportunity for preventing initial lesions from progressing to cavitated decay, or even reversing the disease process, is missed, and disease progresses to cavitated decay where restoration is required. The cornerstone of caries detection is a visual and tactile dental examination, and the ability of clinicians to accurately detect disease in this way has been researched for over half a century. A range of tests exists which may be suitable at different stages of the care pathway, particularly focusing on the detection and diagnosis of disease. Reviews will be completed for each of the following index tests: visual or visual-tactile examination, radiography, fluorescence, electrical conductance, and fiber-optic transillumination. Despite technological advancement, the usual method of caries detection is currently based upon information from visual-tactile clinical examination with or without radiographs. There have been a number of systematic reviews conducted in this area, commencing with an extensive review of in vitro studies investigating visual, radiographic, fiber-optic, electrical conductance, and fluorescence in primary and permanent dentition.
